title: When did consistency become 'follow the PowerPoint'?
author: Brolga Education
summary: This short piece challenges a common conflation in schools that have adopted explicit teaching: treating “consistency” as everyone following the same PowerPoint. The author argues that many teachers were handed slides without ever being shown how to think, act, and respond to students during instruction. When students struggle, the reflexive fixes—add another worked example, another animated slide, explain it once more—make the deck longer and the workload heavier while missing the real problem: no one taught teachers how to make instructional decisions in the moment. Consistency, she contends, should live in shared lesson structure and in-the-moment judgement, not in memorised slides; the piece points readers toward coaching on the thinking behind the template rather than the template itself.
points: Consistency has been quietly redefined as “following the PowerPoint,” when it should mean shared understanding of lesson structure and responsive decision-making.
Many teachers were given slides but never shown how to think, act, and respond to students during explicit teaching.
The default responses to struggle—another worked example, another slide, one more explanation—inflate the deck and the teacher’s workload without addressing the real gap.
The underlying problem is decision-making: nobody has shown teachers what experienced explicit-instruction teachers actually attend to while teaching.
